The Polar Regions Guide: Antarctica, the Arctic, and the Case for the Ends of the Earth

Antarctica, Svalbard, Greenland, Iceland, South Georgia, and Alaska — why polar travel operates on a completely different planning logic than anywhere else, and why the windows are narrower than most people realize.

Home › Travel Journal › Destination Guide › Polar Regions
MS
Mark Sole Founder & Travel Director · Hit Your Mark Travel
Share

Polar travel is not a category of luxury travel. It is a departure from the framework entirely — a different kind of trip that requires a different kind of planning, a different booking lead time, and a different set of expectations about what the destination will ask of you and give back.

The polar regions share one quality that no other destination can replicate: genuine remoteness. Not the managed remoteness of a private island, or the performative remoteness of a mountain lodge with a helipad, but the remoteness of a place where the nearest human infrastructure is hundreds of miles away and the wildlife has never developed a reason to move when you approach. The silence is not an absence — it is the main event.

The planning logic is different in three specific ways. First, the windows are non-negotiable in a way that almost no other destination is: Antarctica operates in a window of roughly five months (November through March), and the best departures within that window sell 12 to 18 months in advance. Miss the window and you wait a year. Second, the vessel or property choice shapes the entire experience — in a way that hotel selection rarely does anywhere else. The difference between a 200-passenger cruise ship and a 100-passenger expedition vessel in Antarctica is not a comfort upgrade; it is a categorically different trip. Third, the purpose of the trip is almost always a single transformative experience — penguins, icebergs, northern lights, a polar bear on sea ice — and everything else (the food, the cabin, the programming) is infrastructure for that encounter, not the encounter itself.

This guide covers six regions across both poles. They share a climate category and almost nothing else: the planning logic for Iceland (accessible year-round, no expedition required) is completely different from Antarctica (narrow window, all-inclusive ship, 12-month lead time), which is different again from Alaska (multi-experience with a road network and fly-in camps in addition to expedition options). We've organized them as six distinct frameworks rather than one continuous polar category — because that is how they should be planned.

"Antarctica is the only continent without a permanent human population, a government, or a city. What that absence produces — the silence, the scale, the wildlife that has never learned to fear the approach of a human being — is unlike anything else available to the traveler. Most people who go once start planning the return trip before the ship has cleared the Drake Passage."

— Mark Sole, Hit Your Mark Travel

The six regions below are organized by planning complexity, from the most expedition-intensive (Antarctica) to the most accessible (Iceland). Each section covers the specific timing logic that matters, the properties and vessels worth building the trip around, and the gateway airports that serve as entry points. Because polar travel is so timing-sensitive, the timing section that follows the regions is particularly important — the difference between the right month and the wrong month in these destinations is larger than almost anywhere else in the world.

Six Regions

Six Polar Frameworks, Six Planning Logics

The polar regions resist consolidation. Antarctica is an expedition continent with a five-month window and no hotels. Iceland is a year-round destination with direct flights from a dozen US cities. Svalbard operates on two completely different seasonal logics — midnight sun in summer, darkness and northern lights in winter. Each of the six regions below requires its own approach before planning can begin.

01
Best Nov–Mar 10–14 days
Antarctica
The Expedition Continent

The only continent without a permanent human population, a government, or a city. Antarctica is accessible exclusively by expedition ship from Ushuaia (the Antarctic Peninsula) or Punta Arenas, during the austral summer window of November through March. The Peninsula is the standard entry — temperate enough for zodiacs, close enough for 10-day itineraries, with penguin colonies, icebergs, and the specific silence of a place the world hasn't reached. The Ross Sea is longer, more remote, and categorically less visited; Weddell Sea expeditions access pack ice and the route of Shackleton's Endurance. Vessel choice shapes the entire trip: the 100-guest range (Le Commandant Charcot, Silver Endeavour, Seabourn Venture) offers access, programming depth, and naturalist expertise that 200-passenger ships cannot replicate. Book 12–18 months in advance for December and January departures, which are the warmest and most stable.

Le Commandant Charcot (Ponant) — nuclear-powered icebreaker; High Arctic and Antarctica; the most technically capable luxury vessel afloat
Seabourn Venture — 132 guests; 2 submarines, helicopters, 24 zodiacs; ultra-luxury expedition standard
Silver Endeavour (Silversea) — 100 guests; all-inclusive; the closest comparison to Seabourn at a different price point
Gateway: USH (Ushuaia, Argentina) via EZE Buenos Aires · PUQ (Punta Arenas, Chile) for Ross Sea departures
02
Jun–Aug / Feb–Mar 3–7 days
Svalbard
Arctic Norway · Dual-Season Destination

An archipelago in the High Arctic, 650 miles north of mainland Norway, operating on two entirely separate seasonal logics. In summer (June through August), the midnight sun runs 24 hours and the wildlife is at peak activity: polar bears on the tundra and ice edges, walrus haul-outs on the beaches, reindeer and Arctic fox in the valleys, and seabird colonies of 30,000+ birds on the sea cliffs. In late winter (February through March), the Arctic darkness and the blue polar light create a different world entirely — northern lights visible across a sky with no competing horizon, polar bear tracks on the sea ice, and snowmobile expeditions to the edge of the polar icecap. Longyearbyen, the main settlement (population 2,400), has regular direct flights from Oslo on SAS (2.5 hours) and a small but serious hotel infrastructure that has improved significantly in recent years.

Isfjord Radio Adventure Hotel — converted historic Arctic radio station at the edge of the ocean; the most remote hotel in the Nordic region
Basecamp Spitsbergen (Longyearbyen) — expedition-focused; the original Svalbard lodge; strongest guide team in town
Funken Lodge (Longyearbyen) — restored industrial building; the most comfortable Longyearbyen base for non-expedition travelers
Gateway: LYR (Longyearbyen) direct from OSL · ~2.5 hrs · SAS year-round
03
Year-Round 5–10 days
Iceland
The Accessible Polar Experience

The most accessible polar destination in the world: direct flights from JFK, BOS, MIA, ORD, LAX, SEA, and a dozen other US cities year-round, with Keflavík 45 minutes from Reykjavík. Iceland operates on two seasonal products that attract genuinely different travelers. Winter (September through March) is the northern lights season — Aurora Borealis forecasting has become reliable enough to structure a 3-night trip around a serious sighting. The Golden Circle, the South Coast (Seljalandsfoss, Skógafoss, the black sand beaches at Reynisfjara), and the Jökulsárlón glacier lagoon are all accessible year-round. Summer (May through August) is midnight sun, the Westfjords at their most navigable, whale watching from Húsavík in the north, and puffin colonies on the Snæfellsnes peninsula. The luxury hotel infrastructure is small but serious — The Retreat at Blue Lagoon is the reference property; Deplar Farm in the north is the most remote and design-forward.

The Retreat at Blue Lagoon — 62 suites; attached to the geothermal spa; the definitive Iceland luxury property; book 6–9 months ahead
Deplar Farm (Troll Peninsula) — 13 rooms on a converted sheep farm on a fjord in north Iceland; helicopter skiing, whale watching, northern lights
ION Adventure Hotel (Nesjavellir) — 45 rooms on a lava field near Þingvellir; Aurora Bar with floor-to-ceiling north-facing windows designed for lights viewing
Gateway: KEF (Keflavík) direct from 15+ US cities · Icelandair, United, American year-round
04
Jun–Sep / Feb–Apr 7–14 days
Greenland
The Ice Sheet Destination

The world's largest island, 85% covered by the Greenland Ice Sheet, with a total population of 57,000 spread across settlements connected by helicopter, boat, and dogsled — there is no road network between towns. Summer (June through September) delivers the Ilulissat Icefjord, a UNESCO World Heritage site where Sermeq Kujalleq — one of the world's fastest-moving glaciers — calves icebergs the size of apartment buildings into a 40-kilometer fjord that empties into Disko Bay. The icebergs drift south past the town for weeks after calving; watching them at midnight under continuous daylight is one of the defining visual experiences in polar travel. Winter (February through April) offers dog sledding on sea ice, northern lights over the ice sheet, and the stillest, quietest version of the Arctic. Greenland requires significantly more advance planning than Iceland or Svalbard — flight connections are through Copenhagen or Reykjavík, accommodation is limited, and the serious activities (fjord expeditions, helicopter landings on the ice sheet) require operators booked months in advance.

Arctic Hotel Ilulissat — positioned above the Ilulissat Icefjord; the primary luxury base for ice fjord access; World of Greenland expedition program
Hotel Arctic (Ilulissat) — igloo suites for northern lights; the more design-forward option in Ilulissat; rooftop deck over the fjord
Ilimanaq Lodge (Ilulissat) — 15 rooms; the most intimate property; accessible by boat; no road connection from Ilulissat town
Gateway: GOH (Nuuk) or ILU (Ilulissat) via CPH (Copenhagen) on Air Greenland · or via KEF (Reykjavík) seasonally
05
Best Oct–Mar 14–21 days
South Georgia & Falklands
The South Atlantic Wildlife Circuit

South Georgia is, by most measures, the greatest wildlife spectacle accessible to non-scientist travelers anywhere on earth. Salisbury Plain holds a breeding colony of 400,000 king penguins — a number that makes no intuitive sense until you are standing on a hillside looking down at a crowd of birds that extends to the horizon in every direction. The elephant seal beaches are operational chaos — eight tons of blubber and testosterone, audible from 500 meters, indifferent to your presence. The albatross colonies nest on the cliffs above Grytviken, where the grave of Ernest Shackleton sits in a small cemetery behind the whaling station museum, within sight of the mountains he crossed on foot after losing the Endurance. The Falkland Islands, typically included in South Atlantic circuits, offer rockhopper and Magellanic penguins, sea lion colonies, and striated caracaras — a bird with the intellectual curiosity and complete fearlessness of a crow, which will walk up to your boot and examine it. The entirety of the South Georgia and Falklands experience is lived on board — the same expedition vessels as Antarctica. There are no hotels on South Georgia; the vessel is the accommodation.

Le Commandant Charcot / Silver Endeavour / Seabourn Venture — same vessels as Antarctica; South Atlantic circuits depart Ushuaia Oct–Mar
Ponant, Quark, Aurora Expeditions — mid-range options running dedicated Falklands/South Georgia circuits, typically 14–21 days
Itinerary note: best combined with Antarctica for 21-day circuits; standalone South Atlantic circuits (no Antarctica) run Oct–Nov before the penguin colonies thin
Gateway: USH (Ushuaia, Argentina) via EZE · MPN (Mount Pleasant, Falklands) via Santiago for standalone Falklands access
06
Jun–Sep (Bears/Glaciers) 7–14 days
Alaska
Denali · Katmai · Kenai · Northern Lights

Alaska is the most logistically layered of the six polar regions — it has a functioning road network (the Parks Highway, the Seward Highway), a small number of fly-in wilderness camps that require bush planes, and a coastal zone with glacier fjords and marine wildlife accessible from Anchorage in a half-day. The three distinct Alaska experiences: Interior (Denali National Park, one of the great mountain silhouettes on earth — visible and cloud-free in June and July about 30% of days; Fairbanks for northern lights September through March), Coastal (Kenai Fjords, where tidewater glaciers calve directly into the ocean and the wildlife boat tours out of Seward are among the most productive in North America for orca, humpback, puffins, and Steller sea lions), and Remote Camps (Katmai National Park for brown bears catching sockeye salmon in mid-leap at Brooks Falls, July through September; Ultima Thule Lodge in Wrangell-St. Elias for glacier landings and ski mountaineering). Katmai's Brooks Falls is the most photographed brown bear viewing site in the world and is genuinely accessible — the NPS boardwalk places you 15 meters from the waterfall and the bears are close enough that the camera autofocus locks on fur. The Alaska northern lights season runs September through March from Fairbanks, which has a clearer aurora window than Svalbard or Iceland in most years.

Ultima Thule Lodge (Wrangell-St. Elias) — accessible only by bush plane; glacier landings, ski mountaineering, river rafting; the most remote Alaska lodge
Camp Denali (Denali National Park) — 18-unit wilderness camp with direct views of Denali; 3–7 night stays; guided natural history program
Winterlake Lodge (Iditarod Trail) — fly-in only; the finest kitchen in Alaska backcountry; positioned for northern lights Sep–Mar and heli-skiing Mar–Apr
Gateway: ANC (Anchorage) direct from JFK/LAX/SEA/ORD/DFW · FAI (Fairbanks) for northern lights, connecting via ANC or SEA
Seasonal Logic

The Windows That Matter — and the Ones to Avoid

Best Window · Antarctica
Nov – Mar
Antarctica & South Georgia Season

The only window the continent is accessible. November is early season — calmer Drake Passage, emperor penguin chick creches on the ice; December and January are warmest and most stable, with 20 hours of light; February and March are late season with leopard seals and the earliest autumn light on the icebergs. Book December–January 12–18 months in advance. South Georgia circuits operate October through March, with October–November best for penguin breeding colony activity.

Best Window · Arctic
Jun – Aug
Arctic Midnight Sun

The prime window for Svalbard (polar bears, walrus, seabird colonies), Greenland (iceberg season, Ilulissat Icefjord at peak), and Alaska (Katmai bears, Kenai Fjords, Denali). Iceland is also excellent June–August for midnight sun, Westfjords access, and whale watching from Húsavík. The 24-hour light is disorienting for two nights and then becomes the reason you came. Expedition ships in the High Arctic run June through September from Longyearbyen; July and August are the warmest and most active wildlife months.

Northern Lights Window
Sep – Mar
Aurora Season — Iceland, Svalbard, Alaska

The northern lights require darkness, clear skies, and solar activity — none of which can be guaranteed, but all of which can be optimized. September through March provides the darkness window across Iceland, Svalbard, and Alaska's interior. February and March have the highest statistical frequency of Aurora Borealis sightings (stable cold air, clear skies, peak solar cycle). Fairbanks, Alaska, has the highest clear-night percentage of the three options in most years. Iceland is the most accessible, with direct US flights and the ability to build a 3-night trip specifically around a forecast sighting.

Avoid / Plan Around
Apr – Oct (Antarctica)
Antarctic Winter — No Access

Antarctica is completely inaccessible from April through October — the polar winter covers the continent in darkness, sea ice locks the access routes, and no commercial expeditions operate. There is no off-season bargain available; the window is the window. The Arctic in winter (October through May, minus Feb–Mar for specific northern lights and Svalbard experiences) is similarly constrained: Greenland fjord access closes with sea ice, Iceland weather becomes genuinely challenging, and Svalbard wildlife visibility drops to near zero without the midnight sun.

Selected Properties & Vessels

Eight Properties and Ships Worth Knowing

In polar travel, the vessel or lodge choice shapes the experience in a way that hotel selection rarely does elsewhere. These eight represent the strongest options across both poles — selected for expedition expertise, access quality, and the degree to which the product is genuinely built around the landscape it operates in.

Le Commandant Charcot
Nuclear Icebreaker
Antarctica · High Arctic · Ponant
The only nuclear-powered luxury expedition vessel in commercial operation — a Ponant ship that can break through 2.5 meters of ice and reach latitudes that no other luxury vessel can access. 245 guests; two helicopters; 30 zodiacs; a Blue Eye underwater observation lounge built into the hull for watching bioluminescence and marine life through submerged portholes; a pool, spa, and two restaurants. The critical operational point: nuclear propulsion means Le Commandant Charcot can operate in the High Arctic (North Pole expeditions) and the Weddell Sea (Endurance route) in addition to the standard Antarctic Peninsula — accessing locations that conventional ice-strengthened ships cannot reach. The product is Ponant's most expensive, and it is priced for what it can do rather than what it looks like. The North Pole expedition (90°N, summer solstice) is one of the rarest itineraries in expedition travel and books years in advance.
Seabourn Venture
Ultra-Luxury
Antarctica · Arctic · Seabourn
132 guests across 132 all-veranda suites; two submarines (the only expedition vessel in the world to carry operational submersibles commercially); two helicopters; 24 zodiacs; a team of 26 expedition staff including marine biologists, ornithologists, glaciologists, and a historian. The Seabourn Venture represents the current benchmark for the ultra-luxury expedition category — the suites are the size of small hotel rooms, the food and wine program is full Seabourn fleet standard, and the expedition programming is credentialed rather than performative. The submarines are the differentiator: they descend to 300 meters and can position beneath icebergs, above seafloor habitats, and alongside kelp forest walls that no zodiac excursion can reach. Pairs with Seabourn Pursuit (identical sister ship launched 2023) for back-to-back Antarctica and Arctic itineraries if the scheduling works.
The Retreat at Blue Lagoon
Geothermal
Grindavík · Reykjanes Peninsula · Iceland
62 suites built into the lava field adjacent to the Blue Lagoon geothermal spa — a Silica Hotel reimagination that opened in 2018 and immediately became the reference Iceland luxury property. Each suite has a private in-suite entrance to the lagoon, which means guests can enter the water at 3am in the middle of winter darkness, under the northern lights, with no one else present. The lagoon is a byproduct of the Svartsengi geothermal power plant; the mineral-rich water (silica, algae, minerals) is at a constant 37–39°C and replenished 40 hours a cycle. The spa is the largest in Iceland. The LAVA restaurant is built into the lava rock of the cliff wall above the lagoon. Keflavík airport is 20 minutes away, which makes The Retreat a logical first or last night on any Iceland itinerary. Book 6–9 months in advance for winter northern lights stays, which fill earliest.
Deplar Farm
Remote Farm
Troll Peninsula · North Iceland · Fljótshlíð Valley
13 rooms on a converted sheep farm in the Fljótshlíð valley, on the Troll Peninsula of north Iceland — 3 hours from Reykjavík, positioned on a fjord with a resident humpback whale population in summer and northern lights visible from the hot tub in winter. The hotel was built with a specific activity program as the product: helicopter skiing on the mountains above the farm in March and April (one of the finest heli-ski operations in Europe, with 1,500–2,000 meters of vertical and no lift queues), whale watching on the fjord in summer, northern lights excursions in winter, and year-round cold water swimming, kayaking, and guided hiking in a valley that no tourist infrastructure has reached. The Icelandic design — corrugated metal exterior, warm timber and stone interior, locally sourced food — is calibrated to the landscape in a way that most remote lodges are not. The 13-room scale means the operation can flex entirely around a small group.
Isfjord Radio
Arctic Station
Cape Linné · Spitsbergen · Svalbard
A historic radio station at the mouth of Isfjorden — the largest fjord in Svalbard — converted to a 98-guest adventure hotel and operating as the most remote hotel in the Nordic region. The site operated as Norway's primary Arctic communication station from 1933 to 1999; the main building, the generator house, and the outbuildings were restored into hotel rooms, a restaurant, a bar, and a library. There is no road connection to Longyearbyen — the hotel is accessible by snowmobile, boat, or helicopter depending on the season. In summer, the site faces 24-hour midnight sun across the fjord toward the Isfjorden glacier; in winter, the northern lights are visible from the original radio tower still standing on the headland. The guide team runs daily wilderness excursions — polar bears are present in the area year-round and the hotel operates strict polar bear watch protocols. The product is expedition-grade infrastructure with hotel comfort — the correct combination for Svalbard.
Ultima Thule Lodge
Fly-In Wilderness
Wrangell–St. Elias National Park · Alaska
A fly-in wilderness lodge on the Chitina River in Wrangell-St. Elias — the largest national park in the US, covering an area larger than Switzerland — accessible only by bush plane from a gravel airstrip near McCarthy. Four cabins and a main lodge, run by the Claus family since 1985, offering an activity program that changes radically by season: ski mountaineering and glacier landings in late winter, float trips on the Chitina and Tana rivers in summer, bear viewing at the salmon streams in August, fall foliage and moose from a float plane in September, and northern lights from the porch in winter. The defining feature of Ultima Thule is the flying: the Bush pilots here are among the best in Alaska, and the glacier landings — setting down on a crevassed river of ice in a Super Cub, engine off, nothing for 20 miles in any direction — are the kind of experience the lodge was built around. Not a luxury spa retreat; a serious wilderness camp with exceptional food and an excellent wine list.
Arctic Hotel Ilulissat
Ice Fjord
Ilulissat · Disko Bay · Greenland
The primary luxury base for the Ilulissat Icefjord — a UNESCO World Heritage site where Sermeq Kujalleq, one of the most productive glaciers in the northern hemisphere, calves icebergs continuously into a 40-kilometer fjord that empties into Disko Bay. The hotel sits on the hill above Ilulissat town, with rooms facing west over the fjord toward the icebergs, which drift south past the hotel for weeks after calving and are visible at any hour under the midnight sun in summer. World of Greenland, the operator attached to the hotel, runs the serious expedition programming: helicopter landings on the ice sheet, boat tours into the icefjord among bergs that reach 100 meters above the waterline, dog sled expeditions on sea ice in winter, and heli-hiking on the moraine ridge above the glacier calving face. The programming is what justifies Ilulissat as a destination; the hotel is the best available infrastructure for accessing it.
Silver Endeavour
Expedition Ship
Antarctica · Arctic · Silversea
Silversea's dedicated expedition vessel — 100 guests across 50 suites, all with private balconies; all-inclusive (flights, transfers, excursions, premium beverages, gratuities); a team of 20 Expedition Team specialists led by a chief expedition officer with documented polar field credentials. Silver Endeavour launched in 2022 as a purpose-built expedition ship rather than a converted cruise vessel — a meaningful distinction in how zodiacs are launched, how shore landings are organized, and how the vessel maneuvers in tight ice. The all-inclusive pricing model changes the Alaska and Antarctica calculation for clients who otherwise resist all-inclusive formats: in a destination where every shore excursion, every zodiac, every kayak, and every flight is otherwise separately ticketed, the bundled price is typically the better value. The on-board food program is full Silversea fleet standard — the wine cellar and the La Dame restaurant (with Relais & Châteaux-certified kitchen) are the best on any expedition vessel currently operating.
